summary: Describes a reference model for Autonomic Networking in managed networks. It defines how an autonomic node behaves, how the elements of an autonomic context work together, and how autonomic services can use the infrastructure.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes how devices in a managed network can establish trust, discover one another, and run network functions with less manual setup. It provides a reference model rather than one complete implementation.

questions: what is the autonomic control plane
subtitle: A reference model for managed networks that automate some of their own functions.

tldr.problem: Managing a network can require extensive manual configuration, while autonomous functions need a consistent way to discover peers and communicate securely.
tldr.mechanism: The model places a common Autonomic Networking Infrastructure beneath Autonomic Service Agents and describes node enrollment, discovery, an Autonomic Control Plane, and trust.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC describes the first phase of a reference model. Several topics marked with an asterisk are research areas outside current implementation specifications.

facts.value: Factory Default, Enrolled, and In ACP

today: RFC 8993 is an Informational reference model published in May 2021. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC identifies related specifications for GRASP, the ACP, and bootstrapping.

sections.title: A Model for Partly Self-Managing Networks
sections.content:
The reference model is intended for professionally managed networks where skilled operators remain involved. It supports a hybrid network: some functions may be autonomic while other functions continue to use traditional management.

The RFC describes a first phase intended to be implementable. Topics marked with an asterisk are considered in the architecture but are not covered by the current implementation specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The model allows a network to automate some functions while people continue to manage others. It is designed for networks that still have human operators.

sections.title: Infrastructure and Service Agents
sections.content:
Each autonomic node implements an Autonomic Networking Infrastructure (ANI), which provides shared functions such as naming, addressing, discovery, signaling, and routing within the Autonomic Control Plane (ACP).

Autonomic Service Agents (ASAs) run above the ANI and implement particular autonomic functions. They use the ANI's services to discover and communicate with other agents.
sections.plainLanguage: Every node provides a common infrastructure for basic network functions. Software agents use that foundation to carry out specific network tasks.

sections.title: The Node Lifecycle
sections.content:
An autonomic node follows three states. In Factory Default, it has a manufacturer-provided IDevID but no domain-specific identity. Successful enrollment gives it a Local Device Identifier (LDevID), moving it to Enrolled.

When the node establishes an ACP channel to another domain node, it enters the In ACP state and can take part in autonomic operations. Losing the last ACP channel returns it to Enrolled. A factory reset removes the LDevID and returns the node to Factory Default.
sections.plainLanguage: A device starts with a manufacturer identity, enrolls in a domain, and then joins its secure control network. If it loses every control-plane channel, it remains enrolled but leaves the active ACP state.

sections.title: Trust and Device Enrollment
sections.content:
The model assumes a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). A Certification Authority is the trust root, and registrars act as Registration Authorities. A new device uses its manufacturer-provided IDevID during enrollment and receives a domain certificate, the LDevID.

The Manufacturer Authorized Signing Authority (MASA) provides ownership tracking and supplies audit, authorization, and ownership tokens during bootstrap. In this phase, devices are treated as fully trusted or fully untrusted within a domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A new device proves its manufacturer identity during enrollment. A registrar then gives it a certificate for the domain so it can authenticate as a member.

sections.title: ASAs and Operator Management
sections.content:
ASAs implement functions on autonomic nodes and communicate through GRASP, the GeneRic Autonomic Signaling Protocol. The RFC lists infrastructure ASAs for enrollment, joining as a proxy for other devices, and establishing the ACP.

Autonomic behavior can coexist with traditional management. When actions conflict, the priority order described here places node-specific management highest, autonomic Intent next, and autonomic default behavior lowest.
sections.plainLanguage: Agents can handle enrollment, secure communication, and other network functions. Operators can still override autonomic behavior through traditional management.
